https://www.jacarandafm.com/shows/breakf.text: Waving flags, "chanting" slogans and marching in circles, around 30 robots took to the streets of Warsaw on Monday to campaign for AI regulation in front of the Polish Digital Affairs Ministry. AFP The protest was organised by Democratism, an initiative that, according to its website, aims to launch debate "on how AI and robotisation affect the labour market". "The robots present here are meant to show that this technology is already a reality," Agibot A3, one of the AI-powered humanoid robots, told AFP. Chants of "Defend workplaces", "Time for rules" and "Don't wait, regulate" played over loudspeakers as the robots, which ranged from bipedal humanoids to dog-like quadrupeds, demonstrated. Robots protest in Warsaw to call for improved AI regulation Around 30 robots march, wave flags and chant slogans outside Poland's digital affairs ministry in Warsaw as part of a demonstration organized by the "Democratism" initiative. The group says it wants to spark debate on… pic.twitter.com/FwT5OFNFFW — The Manila Times (@TheManilaTimes) September 7, 2026 "We particularly want to address the issue of the potential replacement of people both by humanoid robots and by artificial intelligence in cognitive work," organiser Grzegorz Kulis told AFP. "If we don't react now, we may soon have a problem," he added, emphasising the need for "rules and regulations that would serve as a shield protecting workers". Aside from attracting the attention of several passers-by, Kulis said the use of robots was meant to show their existing capabilities and, therefore, the urgency of the situation. "These robots can already move around freely, they're already 'protesting'," he said. The marching robots were met with a visit from Poland's Digital Affairs Minister, Krzysztof Gawkowski, who spoke to Kulis on site. "Uncontrolled (AI) models, implemented into humanoids that will also keep evolving as robotisation moves forward, are a major problem," he said. Kulis, who is now the CIO of a robotics company and CEO of an employment agency, served two terms on the Labour Market Council at the Ministry of Family, Labour and Social Policy. "We feel responsible for starting to inform society about the rapid and dynamic technological changes which personally frighten us," he told AFP. In July, Poland's conservative-nationalist President Karol Nawrocki signed into law a bill put forward by the ministry to implement the EU's AI Act. It created a national authority capable of enforcing existing EU regulations, which had already formally come into force. Tune in to the ' Breakfast with Martin Bester ', weekdays from 06:00 – 09:00. Credit: Anthony Rathbun Kyle Sturdivant is perhaps Houston theater’s most fearless actor. His considerable ego is consumed in Eugène Ionesco’s most famous play, Rhinoceros (1959), as his character, condescending functionary Jean, transforms into a fierce ungulate, stomping the ground, sniffing his friend, frantically searching his forehead for the first hint of a horn, lowering his voice to a bass growl, and balling his fists into what look like hooves. It is a terrifying transformation, horrifying his best friend Berenger (George Parker) who can’t believe what he witnesses. He rushes from Jean’s apartment before he is trampled. Everyone in the small French town is turning into rhinoceros, stampeding through the town square, trumpeting their altered states, wailing for their wives to join them. Calling for everyone to join them. Come, they roar; think no more, be one of us. Ionesco’s classic surreal play is an ironic Aesop fairy tale, moral allegory, and passionate condemnation of the rise of fascism. See how easy it is to conform. Follow without questioning, follow your neighbors, do what they do. We won’t hurt you as long as you don’t question what is happening, as long as you don’t oppose us. As long as you’re not an “other,” a member of the resistance, or a Jew. Ionesco saw this firsthand in Romania and later France. Born in Romania, raised in France, he returned as a teenager to his native Romania after his parents divorced, then returned to France to resume his college studies. But the rise in French antisemitism forced him back to Romania, but there he witnessed the rise of the Romanian Legion of the Archangel Michael, the infamous precursor of the Nazi Iron Guard. At the onset of WWII he left Romania for Marseilles. No one in Europe could run far from the juggernaut. The hideous ideology of the Nazis, and later Communists, profoundly influenced his writing, no more so than in his first full-length play Rhinoceros . After a career as poet and literary critic, his early one-acts like The Bald Soprano (1948) and The Chairs (1952) pushed him to the front of the absurdists with their “anti-play” conventions of repetitive dialogue, non-linear structure, and bizarre situations. But it was Rhinoceros that would cement his reputation among fellow playwrights and, later, audiences. Catastrophic revives one of its signature works starring the magnificent leads from its 2017 production, Sturdivant and Parker, also directed by Tamarie Cooper, with cartoon painted drops designed by Ryan McGettigan, costumes by Macy Lyne out of a Jacques Tati comedy, and Shawn St. John’s tumultuous, thundering sound design. This time the lighting is by Ian Evans. Some of the subsidiary roles repeat: Noel Bowers as the Logician and insufferable Botard; Abraham Zapata as newspaper manager Papillon slowly turning beastly; Karina Pal Montaño-Bowers as the Old Gentleman; Rebecca Randall as Mrs. Boeuf, who jumps down onto her rampaging husband and rides away on his back like Europa on Zeus. Newcomers are: Sara Jo Dunstan, as impatient Fireman; Mara McGhee, whose beloved cat gets flattened in the second rhino attack; Jovan Jackson as intellectual Dudard, Ionesco’s wicked satire of Sartre who acquiesces to the town’s transformation with dispassionate condescension, and Jenna Morris Miller, as innocent love interest Daisy, who turns into a harridan as she succumbs to the rhino’s siren song. Sturdivant is his own force of nature and holds the stage with a magnetism not seen since Mesmer; while Parker, not seen for nine years on Houston stages, has been sorely missed. His Berenger, Ionesco’s avatar Everyman, morphs anxiety into the very stuff of drama, almost going mad from his reluctance to become like everybody else. His final defiance, “I’m not capitulating,” ends the play with a blackout. His humanity, which includes his sloven demeanor, his alcoholism, his passive aggressiveness, even his cowardice, will save him, promises Ionesco. Defy, defy, defy. Stay human and flawed, and the beasts of the mob might just remain outside the door. Rhinoceros continues through October 10 at 7:30 p.m. Monday, October 5, and Thursdays; 8 p.m. Fridays and Saturdays; and 2:30 p.m. Sundays at Catastrophic Theatre at MATCH, 3400 Main. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Meghan Markle said her thoughts were ‘with any children who may have been harmed’. Photograph: Getty View image in fullscreen Meghan Markle said her thoughts were ‘with any children who may have been harmed’. Photograph: Getty Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex Duchess of Sussex ‘deeply distressed’ over child sexual abuse image claims against father Meghan reveals she was made aware of ‘disturbing allegations’ against him in 2018 by Met police Caroline Davies Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.16 EDT First published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 06.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Duchess of Sussex has said she is “deeply distressed” over accusations involving child sexual abuse images against her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, and revealed she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018 by the Metropolitan police. Meghan issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother Thomas Markle Jr alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines. In an interview with the Daily Mail, Markle Sr denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick lies”. It is understood that authorities in the UK previously told Meghan that allegations made about her father in a 2018 letter sent to Scotland Yard, and subsequently shared with her by the police, were being investigated. Meghan was informed by the Met of the allegations in the summer shortly after her wedding, it is believed. In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed. “In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection [Rasp]. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families. “Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.” The 2018 letter was understood to have been shared with Meghan by the Rasp unit within the Met police. It is understood the Met has not previously investigated Markle Snr, nor is it currently doing so. The force said it was making internal inquiries regarding officers from Rasp being involved in the passing on of a letter. A Met spokesperson said: “We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met’s royalty and specialist protection command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018. We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this.” Markle Sr has been estranged from the duchess since he failed to attend her wedding to Prince Harry on health grounds, and he has never met his grandchildren Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke. Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported. The undersecretary for the Philippines’ justice department, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC the matter was being investigated by a human trafficking and child sexual exploitation taskforce in Cebu. The interior secretary, Jonvic Remulla, separately told the BBC that national police had secured Markle Sr’s computer to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination. Remulla said it would take “one week to get the forensic [results]”. Meghan’s father has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail that the accusations were “sick lies”. He told the newspaper that the computers had not been in his possession since he left Rosarito, Mexico, with his son in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”. Speaking from a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk with a prosthetic limb after his left leg was amputated because of a blood clot, he told the Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of. “This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.” Meghan’s half-sister Samantha Markle has defended their father, accusing her brother Markle Jr of “making up lies” to make money. She told the Mail: “There is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever and my brother is disgusting for making them up. He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.” She alleged her brother made the allegations days after their father cut off his funds, “and once the money stopped he made up the most outrageous lies he could to make money from the media”. She alleged the computers were not in her father’s possession for two years and he could have been set up. “That leaves a lot of room for tampering,” she said.
